{{short description|Q-analog of the ordinary derivative}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''q''-derivative}}
In [[mathematics]], in the area of [[combinatorics]] and [[quantum calculus]], the '''''q''-derivative''', or '''Jackson derivative''', is a [[q-analog|''q''-analog]] of the [[ordinary derivative]], introduced by [[Frank Hilton Jackson]]. It is the inverse of [[Jackson integral|Jackson's ''q''-integration]]. For other forms of q-derivative, see {{harvtxt|Chung|Chung|Nam|Kang|1994}}.

==Definition==
The ''q''-derivative of a function ''f''(''x'') is defined as{{sfn|Jackson|1908|pp=253–281}}{{sfn|Kac|Pokman Cheung|2002}}{{sfn|Ernst|2012}}

<math display="block">\left(\frac{d}{dx}\right)_q f(x)=\frac{f(qx)-f(x)}{qx-x}.</math>

It is also often written as <math>D_qf(x)</math>. The ''q''-derivative is also known as the '''Jackson derivative'''.

Formally, in terms of Lagrange's [[shift operator]] in logarithmic variables, it amounts to the operator
<math display="block">D_q= \frac{1}{x} ~ \frac{q^{d~~~ \over d (\ln x)}  -1}{q-1} ~, </math>
which goes to the plain derivative, <math>D_q \to \frac{d}{dx}</math> as <math>q \to 1</math>.

It is manifestly linear,
<math display="block">\displaystyle D_q (f(x)+g(x)) = D_q f(x) + D_q g(x)~.</math>

It has a [[product rule]] analogous to the ordinary derivative product rule, with two equivalent forms

<math display="block">\displaystyle D_q (f(x)g(x)) = g(x)D_q f(x) + f(qx)D_q g(x) = g(qx)D_q f(x) + f(x)D_q g(x). </math>

Similarly, it satisfies a [[quotient rule]],

<math display="block">\displaystyle D_q (f(x)/g(x)) = \frac{g(x)D_q f(x) - f(x)D_q g(x)}{g(qx)g(x)},\quad g(x)g(qx)\neq 0. </math>

There is also a rule similar to the chain rule for ordinary derivatives. Let <math>g(x) = c x^k</math>. Then

<math display="block">\displaystyle D_q f(g(x)) = D_{q^k}(f)(g(x))D_q(g)(x).</math>

The [[eigenfunction]] of the ''q''-derivative is the [[q-exponential|''q''-exponential]] ''e<sub>q</sub>''(''x'').

==Relationship to ordinary derivatives==
''Q''-differentiation resembles ordinary differentiation, with curious differences. For example, the ''q''-derivative of the [[monomial]] is:{{sfn|Kac|Pokman Cheung|2002}}

<math display="block">\left(\frac{d}{dz}\right)_q z^n = \frac{1-q^n}{1-q} z^{n-1} =
[n]_q z^{n-1}</math>

where <math>[n]_q</math> is the [[q-bracket|''q''-bracket]] of ''n''. Note that <math>\lim_{q\to 1}[n]_q = n</math> so the ordinary derivative is regained in this limit.

The ''n''-th ''q''-derivative of a function may be given as:{{sfn|Ernst|2012}}

<math display="block">(D^n_q f)(0)=
\frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!} \frac{(q;q)_n}{(1-q)^n}=
\frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!} [n]!_q
</math>

provided that the ordinary ''n''-th derivative of ''f'' exists at ''x'' = 0. Here, <math>(q;q)_n</math> is the [[q-Pochhammer symbol|''q''-Pochhammer symbol]], and <math>[n]!_q</math> is the [[q-factorial|''q''-factorial]]. If <math>f(x)</math> is [[Analytic function|analytic]] we can apply the [[Taylor's theorem|Taylor formula]] to the definition of <math>D_q(f(x)) </math> to get

<math display="block">\displaystyle D_q(f(x)) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(q-1)^k}{(k+1)!} x^k f^{(k+1)}(x).</math>

A ''q''-analog of the Taylor expansion of a function about zero follows:{{sfn|Kac|Pokman Cheung|2002}}

<math display="block">f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty f^{(n)}(0)\,\frac{z^n}{n!} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (D^n_q f)(0)\,\frac{z^n}{[n]!_q}.</math>

==Higher order ''q''-derivatives==
The following representation for higher order <math>q</math>-derivatives is known:{{sfn|Koepf|2014}}{{sfn|Koepf|Rajković|Marinković|2007|pp=621–638}}
<math display="block">D_q^nf(x)=\frac{1}{(1-q)^nx^n}\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}_q q^{\binom{k}{2}-(n-1)k}f(q^kx).</math>
<math>\binom{n}{k}_q</math> is the <math>q</math>-binomial coefficient. By changing the order of summation as <math>r=n-k</math>, we obtain the next formula:{{sfn|Koepf|2014}}{{sfn|Annaby|Mansour|2008|pp=472–483}}
<math display="block">D_q^nf(x)=\frac{(-1)^n q^{-\binom{n}{2}}}{(1-q)^nx^n}\sum_{r=0}^n(-1)^r\binom{n}{r}_q q^{\binom{r}{2}}f(q^{n-r}x).</math>

Higher order <math>q</math>-derivatives are used to <math>q</math>-Taylor formula and the <math>q</math>-[[Rodrigues' formula]] (the formula used to construct <math>q</math>-[[orthogonal polynomials]]{{sfn|Koepf|2014}}).

==Generalizations==
===Post Quantum Calculus===
Post quantum calculus is a generalization of the theory of [[quantum calculus]], and it uses the following operator:<ref>Gupta V., Rassias T.M., Agrawal P.N., Acu A.M. (2018) Basics of Post-Quantum Calculus. In: Recent Advances in Constructive Approximation Theory. SpringerOptimization and Its Applications, vol 138. Springer.</ref>{{sfn|Duran|2016}}
<math display="block">D_{p,q}f(x):=\frac{f(px)-f(qx)}{(p-q)x},\quad x\neq 0.</math>

===Hahn difference===
[[Wolfgang Hahn]] introduced the following operator (Hahn difference):<ref>Hahn, W. (1949). Math. Nachr. 2: 4-34.</ref><ref>Hahn, W. (1983) Monatshefte Math. 95: 19-24.</ref>
<math display="block">D_{q,\omega}f(x):=\frac{f(qx+\omega)-f(x)}{(q-1)x+\omega},\quad 0<q<1,\quad\omega>0.</math>

When <math>\omega\to0</math> this operator reduces to <math>q</math>-derivative, and when <math>q\to1</math> it reduces to forward difference. This is a successful tool for constructing families of [[orthogonal polynomials]] and investigating some approximation problems.{{sfn|Foupouagnigni|1998}}<ref>Kwon, K.; Lee, D.; Park, S.; Yoo, B.: ''Kyungpook Math. J.'' 38, 259-281 (1998).</ref><ref>Alvarez-Nodarse, R.: J. Comput. Appl. Math. 196, 320-337 (2006).</ref>

===''β''-derivative===
<math>\beta</math>-derivative is an operator defined as follows:<ref>Auch, T. (2013): ''Development and Application of Difference and Fractional Calculus on Discrete Time Scales''. PhD thesis, University of Nebraska-Lincoln.</ref>{{sfn|Hamza|Sarhan|Shehata|Aldwoah|2015|p=182}}
<math display="block">D_\beta f(t):=\frac{f(\beta(t))-f(t)}{\beta(t)-t},\quad\beta\neq t,\quad\beta:I\to I.</math>

In the definition, <math>I</math> is a given interval, and <math>\beta(t)</math> is any [[continuous function]] that strictly monotonically increases (i.e. <math>t>s\rightarrow\beta(t)>\beta(s)</math>). When <math>\beta(t)=qt</math> then this operator is <math>q</math>-derivative, and when <math>\beta(t)=qt+\omega</math> this operator is Hahn difference.

== Applications ==
The q-calculus has been used in machine learning for designing stochastic activation functions.{{sfn|Nielsen|Sun|2021|pp=2782–2789}}
